Market Note 02 · The learning series

Falling inflation does not necessarily mean falling prices

A slower increase still leaves prices rising. Follow one basket to see the distinction.

3-minute read · Evergreen educational draft

A rate of change is not a price level

“Inflation is falling” can sound like “the shopping bill is falling.” It usually means something different: the average price level is still rising, but more slowly. Inflation measures a change in prices; the price level describes how high those prices are. De Nederlandsche Bank makes this distinction explicit.

Think of the price level as your position on a staircase and inflation as how quickly you climb. Slowing down does not move you back to the bottom. Prices can remain much higher than a few years ago even after inflation eases.

An illustrative basket: 100 → 110 → 115.5

Start with a fictional price index of 100. After one year of 10% inflation, it reaches 110. If inflation then falls to 5%, the next year’s level becomes 115.5: 110 × 1.05.

Inflation has slowed from 10% to 5%, a fall of five percentage points. Yet the basket is 5% more expensive than a year earlier and 15.5% more expensive than at the start. The rates compound: adding 10% and 5% would incorrectly give 15%.

This is an arithmetic illustration, not an observation about any country or household. It demonstrates why slower inflation can coexist with continued pressure on a budget.

Disinflation and deflation are different

Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate. Our move from positive 10% to positive 5% is disinflation. Deflation means a decline in the broad price level: negative inflation over the measured period. A lower price for one item, such as petrol, does not establish economy-wide deflation. These distinctions are explained by Federal Reserve Education.

Why your own shopping bill may feel different

An official inflation index averages a basket of goods and services, with larger spending categories carrying more weight. Individual households buy different things. Rent, food or energy might take a bigger share of your budget than of the average basket, so your experience can differ from the headline rate. The European Central Bank explains both weighting and household differences.

The comparison period matters too. An annual rate compares a month with the same month a year earlier. A monthly rate compares it with the previous month. Annual inflation can ease partly because unusually high earlier price increases leave that comparison window. That alone does not prove prices fell this month.

How to read the next inflation headline

Check three things: the reference period, the basket being measured, and whether the reported change concerns the inflation rate or the price level. If the headline rate falls, ask which components drove it and whether the improvement is broad.

For equity analysis, slower cost growth could help margins, while weaker demand could hurt revenue. Those are channels to investigate, not automatic market outcomes. One inflation number does not tell you what investors expected, how companies will respond, or whether an index should rise.

Keep the distinction

100 → 110 → 115.5

Year 1: +10%. Year 2: +5%. The rate slows; the price level still rises. Fictional index, not market data.
